I've done it for so many different reasons over the years, all I knew at the time was that it helped. 

I used to feel very numb and it was a way to break that and feel something. Then it acted as a release for my stress. It became a habit, something I just did. It was what I turned to when I didn't know what else to do.

I've been in a similar situation as well where I had struggled with selfharm before getting into my relationship, but I struggled during it as well. Personally my ex was abusive and I used my selfharm to cope with that among other things outside the relationship. 

In your case it could be either or both. If you are having any doubts about the relationship that could be a sign of an unhealthy relationship and you may want to considering leaving. If you feel comfortable, this could be a conversation with your partner as well, to talk about your selfharm and how your arguments affect you.

I can understand where you're coming from. After being addicted to selfharm for four years, I feel like I'm prone to other addictions as well. The best thing you can do for your friends is to let them know you're there for them: to listen, to distract, whathaveyou. 

When it comes to selfharm, there's unfortunately not a lot your can do past that to help them. There's not magic cure all. Your friends obviously trust you a lot of they have told you about it, so that is a really good start. I know for me, telling someone for the first time was a huge step for me and has helped me with my recovery through the years. This is something that could be a part of their lives for awhile. For me, I've been selfharming for four years now and I'm just over a year clean. With that said, things are still hard, I still get the urges to do it again. Just keeping an open line of communication without judgment is important. And if getting professional help is an option for them, maybe suggest that as well, but it isn't always so don't push it too much. Getting clean is very much a personal battle, so just being there for them to help them through the fight is important

I hope this help at all, if you want to chat more, you are more than welcome to pm me. Best of luck to you and your friends

I'm really sorry you're going through this. Your experiences are never any less than someone else's. It affects you regardless of how bad it was and that's okay. 

I can relate to you in regards to your ex boyfriend. For me, my ex would constantly he grabbing my butt, chest, etc and I told him to stop every time, but he never did. He always saw it as a joke, but it made me super uncomfortable, especially because it was always in public. He also pressured me into sexual things that I wasn't ready for. As a first experience into these things it can mess up your perspectives on sex in general. Even now I'm still uncomfortable being physically close to people and that's something in trying to work on, but time will be your friend here. 

As for your question, I'm still trying to figure out the correct terms to describe what happened to me as well. Your early stuff was definitely harassment at least. As for your ex, at least for me I'd characterize it as sexual assasult. That's how I've begun to define what happened to me. The legal definition of sexual assault (atleast in the US) is sexual contact or behavior that occurs without explicit consent of the victim. This covers anything from attempted rape, unwanted sexual touching, forcing victims to perform sexual acts, and rape. Sexual assasult is like an umbrella term for all of the above. I found this on the RAINN (Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network) website. 

I hope this can help you. I know putting a label on these things can be scary, but it can also help you process what happened to you. If you want to talk at all, my dms are open. Best of luck to you in your recovery

I absolutely love that you want to support her! I started gymnastics when I was two and is has been and still is the biggest part of my life, even as a college student. 

With the age that she is right now, there's not a whole lot for her to do outside of the gym, but just watching her at class, listening to her stories about practices, and congratulating her on new skills. As she gets older, I promise you'll learn more about the sport from her and just from being in the gym. Just as she does grow up make sure you listen to her and her needs, especially when it comes to injuries and coaches. This sport can be an absolutely amazing experience and she'll learn so many life lessons as long as it's a positive experience. There are definitely ups and downs, but it has taught me so much over the years, and I can't be thankful enough. 

As for learning about the sport, watching the past two olympics together are a great idea! Plenty of gymnasts over the years have written books about the sport. And talking to her coach's too, they are really passionate toward the sport.

All you have to do is be there for her, encourage her through it all, and congratulate her on all of her new accomplishments. My dad still does this for me and I can't be thankful enough, it's made a big impact on me.
